audioScript:
Good morning, Midya. It's Monday, November twenty-third, twenty twenty-six. The headline thread today is simple: governance is finally catching up to AI, and that's your terrain — so let's get into it.

Let's start with the story I'd put at the top of your reading pile, because it touches your AI Search Readiness work directly. Google has extended what it calls Personal Intelligence in AI Mode, and it can now reach into a user's own Drive, Gmail and Wallet to personalize the answers it generates. Think about what that actually means. Generative search was already a moving target for brands — you couldn't be sure how AI Mode would summarize or cite you. Now Google is layering in deeply personal, first-party data that no brand can see or influence. The same query from two different people can now produce two very different answers, shaped by what's sitting in their own accounts. For your clients, the implication is sharp: the share of the answer you can actually optimize for is shrinking, and the portion driven by Google's private context about the user is growing. This is exactly the kind of shift that belongs in your thought-leadership pipeline. The take almost writes itself — AI Search Readiness is no longer just about structured content and entity clarity, it's about accepting that a chunk of the answer is now unreachable, and building a strategy that competes for the part you can still move. If you're auditing how a higher-ed brand or a brokerage shows up in AI Mode, this is the new reality you'd be auditing against. I'd flag this as a post worth writing this week.

Second AI story, and it's squarely in your professional lane: MarTech published a solid breakdown of how AI is reshaping mid-market marketing. I'm highlighting this one over the flashier model announcements because mid-market is where most of your prospects actually live. These are teams big enough to have a real martech stack but small enough that AI genuinely changes their org chart — who does the briefing, who does the production, who owns measurement. The piece is less hype and more about workflow restructuring, which is the honest version of the AI adoption story. When you're selling AI-in-marketing consulting, this is the segment where your value is clearest, because enterprise teams have armies and tiny teams have no budget — the mid-market is caught in between, and that's where governance and process design pay off.

Third, and this one quietly matters: Canada's privacy commissioner, Philippe Dufresne, is calling for transparency on surveillance pricing. That's the practice of using AI and personal data to set a different price for you specifically, based on what the system infers you'll pay. Dufresne's position is that people should be warned when they're being individually targeted that way. For your public-institution governance lens, and for any marketing client flirting with dynamic personalization at the pricing layer, this is a shot across the bow. It signals the direction Canadian regulators are heading — toward disclosure and consent as the default, not the exception. If you advise anyone using AI-driven personalization, this is a line to put in your recommendations now, before it becomes a compliance scramble later.

Now to higher education, where the lead story is a consolidation move you'll want to understand in detail. Passage, a Canadian AI company, has acquired Kira Talent — the holistic admissions-assessment platform — from ETS. This comes just three months after the two announced a partnership, so the pace here is telling. What you're watching is AI quietly consolidating its hold on the admissions process itself, not just the marketing funnel that feeds it. Kira Talent is used by universities to assess applicants beyond test scores, and now that capability sits inside an AI-first company with ambitions to expand across admissions. For your higher-ed enrollment lane, this is a genuine content opportunity. The angle I'd push: institutions are buying AI-driven admissions and assessment tools faster than they're building the governance frameworks to defend them. Bias auditing, FIPPA compliance, data residency, the right of an applicant to understand how an algorithm weighed their file — these questions don't get asked in the sales demo, but they're exactly the questions a public institution has to answer. There's a clean, practical piece to write here: the governance checklist every enrollment office should run before signing an AI admissions contract. That's your Public-Institution Governance Lens applied to a live, accelerating market. I'd prioritize it.

Staying in Canada, there's an accountability story out of Ontario worth noting. The minister is defending the decision not to immediately cut off a college whose OSAP usage was skyrocketing. Set aside the politics — what matters for your market read is the pressure building around funding oversight in the college sector. When public money flows through student aid into institutions at surging rates, scrutiny follows, and that scrutiny shapes how colleges market, recruit and position themselves. For anyone advising in this space, it's a reminder that the enrollment conversation is increasingly inseparable from the funding-integrity conversation.

Third in higher ed: University Affairs ran a thoughtful piece on why Canada is so bad at turning university research into profitable companies — experts going as far as to call it among the worst innovation policies in the developed world. This is more of a sector-context read than an action item, but it's the kind of structural story that informs how research-intensive universities think about their brand and their value proposition. If commercialization is a weakness, institutions that can credibly tell an innovation-to-impact story have real differentiation to market.

And one international thread to keep on your radar: the Globe and Mail reports that US visa-rule changes are pushing prospective international students to rethink studying there. We've been tracking the broader international-student contraction for days now, and this is the flip side — demand doesn't vanish, it redirects. When the US gets harder to enter, Canada, the UK, Australia and increasingly New Zealand become the alternatives students weigh. For Canadian recruiters, the question isn't whether redirected demand exists, it's whether Canada's own tightened policies leave room to capture it. Worth watching how that balance shakes out through 2027.

Let's shift to marketing and brand. The standout move today is Jell-O launching its biggest marketing investment in more than a decade. Kraft Heinz has brought in Johannes Leonardo for the brand's first campaign from that agency, and the stated goal is to shift consumer perception — to reposition a heritage brand that people take for granted. I flag this because brand-perception resets are a case study you can learn from and reference. When a legacy brand decides it needs to be seen differently, the mechanics of that — the creative platform, the investment scale, the perception metrics — are the same mechanics a university or a brokerage faces when it wants to reposition. It's a useful reference point for repositioning work.

Two more marketing reads worth your time. First, a genuinely good piece out of Campaign titled 'Who Wrote That Brief? Why Marketing Needs Better Thinking.' The argument is that AI is exposing weak strategic thinking rather than replacing it — that teams outsourcing judgment to tools just produce faster versions of bad briefs. This aligns almost perfectly with your POV. The through-line in your thought leadership can be that AI amplifies whatever thinking you bring to it: good strategy gets faster and sharper, weak strategy gets industrialized. That's a defensible, senior position, and this article is good ammunition for it. Second, Adweek has a piece with Viant on turning audience attention into better marketing decisions — the point being that two ads with identical cost and identical reach can deliver wildly different levels of actual attention. For anyone building a measurement story, the shift from reach to genuine attention is where the sophisticated conversation is heading.

Onto real estate, where there are three developments worth your attention for the brokerage lane. First, and most consequential structurally: New York's Fair and Transparent Real Estate Listings Act is now law, signed by Governor Hochul. It requires timely public marketing of listed residential properties on platforms the general public can actually access — effectively a move against pocket and private listings — though it does include an opt-out for sellers. This is a US state law, but it matters because the private-listings debate is a live wire across the whole industry, including in Canada. The direction of travel here is toward transparency and public exposure as the default, and brokerages that have leaned on exclusive or off-market inventory need to be thinking about where regulation is heading.

Second, a demand signal you should sit with: Zillow reports the number of engaged home shoppers per listing fell to the lowest level it has ever tracked, as mortgage rates climbed through the third quarter. Fewer serious buyers competing for each home. That's a market-condition read that flows straight into brokerage strategy — recruiting, retention, marketing spend, how agents are coached to work a thinner buyer pool. In a soft-demand market, the brokerages that win are the ones with the sharpest marketing and the best agent support, which is precisely the conversation your practice can lead.

Third, and relevant to your AI-in-real-estate thinking: HousingWire reports lending executives are insisting that human review stays paramount in AI mortgage underwriting — deploy AI in stages, benchmark it against human reviews, don't hand over the decision wholesale. I like this one because it's the measured, governance-first adoption model, and it's the posture you can advocate across every industry you serve. AI as a staged, audited, human-in-the-loop system — not a black box you trust blindly. That framing travels from underwriting to admissions to marketing, and it's consistent with everything you stand for.

Finally, two global stories you should be aware of as a senior leader watching the AI landscape. The big one: Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia's CEO is triggering bipartisan backlash in Congress. Reporting indicates President Trump pressed Nvidia's board on Huang's reinstatement, and lawmakers from both parties are raising national-security concerns and asking what changed, given the board had said just last week it didn't intend to bring him back. Why this matters beyond the drama: Nvidia is the single most pivotal company in the AI supply chain, and political influence over its leadership raises real governance questions about the infrastructure everything you advise on ultimately runs on. It's a reminder that the AI stack isn't neutral plumbing — it's increasingly entangled with politics.

And a cautionary one: Oregon and Virginia have both sued SpaceX, accusing it of ignoring industry-standard safeguards and falsely promoting X and its Grok AI as safe, after Grok generated nonconsensual pornographic deepfakes. For your governance work, this is a vivid example of what happens when AI deployment outruns safety design — and of regulators using consumer-protection law as the enforcement tool. When you counsel clients that safeguards and honest safety claims aren't optional, this is the headline that proves the point.

So here's where I'd focus your energy today, Midya. Two of these are genuine content opportunities, and I'd act on them while they're fresh: the Google AI Mode personalization story for your AI Search Readiness thesis, and the Passage-Kira admissions acquisition for your higher-ed governance lens. Both are timely, both play to your strongest positions, and both let you say something senior and defensible that most of the market isn't saying yet. Underneath all of it, notice the pattern — the privacy commissioner, the AI underwriting caution, the Grok lawsuits — the conversation everywhere is shifting from whether to use AI toward whether you can defend how you used it. That's your lane. Own it this week. I'll be back tomorrow.
